newsitem.title: USA: U.S. probes Iran deal that may provoke sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. probes Iran deal that may provoke sanctions.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday it was investigating whether sanctions should be imposed on a British-Canadian consortium under U.S. law for a deal with Iran to develop the Balal oil field.

"That's a very serious issue. And we're looking into it with great care right now, but we have not yet made a determination if this particular deal fits that category," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
Under U.S. law, companies investing more than $40 million in any one year in Iranian or Libyan oil and gas projects could be subject to a broad array of trade and financial penalties.

"And our law is very clear. The Iran-Libya Sanctions Act sets a threshold for investment beyond which companies are technically in violation, and therefore can be subject to U.S. penalties," Burns said.
Iran's oil minister on Saturday confirmed that Teheran had awarded a contract to British and Canadian firms to develop the Balal offshore field. The project could cost $140 million or more.

The minister, Gholamreza Aghazadeh, refused to name the two firms but sources at the National Iranian Oil Company identified them as Britain's Pell Frischmann and Canada's Bow Valley. U.S. officials said those were the firms being referred to by Burns.
The spokesman said the Clinton administration planned to seek information about the deal "from the British company, from the UK (United Kingdom), and from other sources."

So far, the United States has not penalised any companies under the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act (ILSA), which was enacted in August 1996 in an effort to deter what President Bill Clinton and other officials say is the two states' support of terrorism.
But 11 projects that Iran said in 1995 were open for bids from foreign firms are also being investigated by the United States in case they violate the law.
"We're looking at this very carefully but have not made a determination yet," one U.S. official said.
He argued that even without any sanctions being imposed the law has been effective because it has discouraged foreign investment in Iran.
But some experts have faulted the United States for not acting already to impose sanctions on companies that have announced deals with Iran.
Hillary Mann of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy said Washington's failure to act so far has fuelled doubts about its willingness to vigorously enforce the sanctions.

"While there is no doubt that the mere passage of ILSA has been a powerful deterrent to companies interested in investing in Iran, the credibility on which that deterrent depends will, over time, be increasingly at risk," she wrote in a recent analysis of the law.

She argued that a recent German court decision that Iran's top leaders ordered the assassination of several dissidents in Berlin has created an opportunity for the United States to re-energise its policy of containment toward Iran.

"Washington should make it clear at the highest levels that the U.S. intends to enforce ILSA vigorously to deter further investment in Iran and to make Iran's leaders actually pay a real economic price for their sponsorship of international terrorism," she wrote.
